stories.headline: Europe and Gulf ministers tell the US: talk, don't strike Iran
body: Foreign ministers from eight countries, including the UK, France, Germany and Saudi Arabia, met in Istanbul on Friday.
They said nobody in the room supports another attack on Iran, and that only talks can end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
But the US ambassador to Türkiye said a US strike could come as soon as this weekend.
stories.joke: Eight ministers, one message: please use your words.
stories.vc: Brent crude touched about $117 this week on this war. High oil means costlier inputs and freight for manufacturers, and nervous investors everywhere.

stories.headline: Brazil picks a president today in a too-close-to-call run-off
body: Brazil votes today, 25 October, in a run-off between Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, and President Lula, 80.
In the first round Bolsonaro got about 47% and Lula just over 45%.
Recent polls show Bolsonaro slightly ahead, but inside the margin of error, so it could go either way.
stories.joke: Polls say 'within the margin of error', which is pollster for 'no idea'.
stories.vc: Brazil is Latin America's biggest market. Bolsonaro promises spending cuts and a debt ceiling; Lula points to lower unemployment. Watch the currency and rates after the result.

stories.headline: First Ebola vaccine trial starts in DR Congo's worst outbreak
body: The WHO has started a vaccine trial in DR Congo, where the worst Ebola outbreak on record has passed 9,700 cases and 4,600 deaths.
The virus has reached four African countries, its widest spread on the continent so far.
The approved vaccine targets a different Ebola type, so new shots from Oxford and Moderna will join the trial soon.
stories.vc: Speed of new vaccine platforms (like mRNA) is the real story. Funders like CEPI back them, and that shapes where health-tech money goes.

stories.headline: Investors rush into Jio Platforms' $3.2 billion IPO
body: Jio Platforms' ₹30,213 crore (about $3.2 billion) IPO closed on Thursday with bids for 22 times the shares on offer.
Big institutions were hungriest, bidding about 70 times their quota; small investors bid about 2.7 times.
At the top price, Jio is valued at around ₹10.3 lakh crore, roughly $108 billion.
stories.joke: Institutions bid 70x, retail 2.7x. Guess who gets the bigger slice of the cake.
stories.vc: All of it is fresh money, with no existing shareholders selling. It shows India's market can absorb giant tech listings, which keeps the IPO exit door open for late-stage VCs.

stories.headline: Swiggy hits a 52-week low as Instamart losses grow
body: Swiggy shares fell about 16% on Thursday to ₹176.70, a 52-week low, after its July–September results.
Its loss was ₹922 crore, more than the ₹791 crore of the quarter before, even though revenue grew 36% from last year.
The worry is Instamart, its quick-delivery arm, where losses widened while rival Blinkit keeps pushing.
stories.vc: Food delivery makes money; quick commerce burns it. The stock is now about 55% below its ₹390 IPO price, a reminder that listing day is not the finish line.

stories.headline: Bengaluru's Tonbo Imaging jumps 62% on market debut
body: Bengaluru defence-tech firm Tonbo Imaging closed its first trading day at about ₹1,134, 62% above its ₹700 IPO price.
It makes thermal cameras, gun sights and missile seekers, and says it supplied about 20,000 of India's roughly 30,000 thermal sights.
But revenue fell about 23% in FY26, and the ₹852 crore IPO was only existing investors selling shares.
stories.joke: Thermal cameras spotted one hot thing on Thursday: their own stock.
stories.vc: The IPO was subscribed about 136 times. Defence tech is India's hottest theme, but at roughly 79x last year's profit at IPO price, early backers chose a good moment to cash out.

stories.headline: FT Unhedged: the bond market's rough year that few noticed
body: On the FT's Unhedged podcast, Robin Wigglesworth explains why government bonds had a rocky year that most people missed.
Bond prices set the interest rates for almost everything, from home loans to company debt.
The hosts also note the UK now has the highest borrowing costs in the G7, so its 28 October budget aims to be boring.
stories.joke: A boring budget: the only speech where a finance minister wants zero applause.
stories.vc: When safe government bonds pay more, investors demand more from risky bets like startups. Higher bond yields quietly push valuations down.

stories.headline: White House plans to curb US–China biotech deals
body: Dan Primack's Pro Rata leads with a White House plan to limit deals between US and Chinese biotech companies over security worries.
It would cover investments, loans and joint ventures for nearly all drugs, plus tools like brain-computer interfaces; licensing deals seem exempt.
Nothing changes before comments close on 7 December, and the final rules may be softer.
stories.joke: Cross-border biotech, now with extra paperwork.
stories.vc: If US drug makers must look beyond China, non-China partners could gain. Indian contract manufacturers are worth watching.

stories.headline: Daytona, a cloud for AI agents, becomes a unicorn
body: Daytona, a three-year-old New York startup, raised a $60 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation, led by FirstMark Growth.
It gives each AI agent its own safe computer to work in, with Linux, Windows, macOS or GPUs.
Its angel investors include the founders of Stripe, Shopify, Perplexity and Zoom.
stories.joke: AI agents now get their own computers. Many interns still don't.
stories.vc: This is a 'picks and shovels' bet: sell the tools every AI agent needs. FirstMark led both its February round and this one, which signals strong insider belief.

stories.headline: Ben Thompson brings in Stripe as Stratechery's sole sponsor
body: Ben Thompson made Stripe the only sponsor of Stratechery, his paid tech newsletter.
He calls mixing subscriptions with ads a 'unified' content business, and says his contract keeps him fully independent.
His Sharp Tech podcast is also becoming a free video show on YouTube.
stories.joke: Even the man who explains business models needed a new business model.
stories.vc: A strong lesson for a future VC: build a trusted audience first, then earn from it twice. Your own reputation is the best deal-flow engine.

stories.headline: The Economist: Europe's centrist leaders are failing voters
body: This week's Economist cover is titled 'The agony of liberal Europe'.
It says Europe's centrist leaders have fallen badly short, as angry voters protest high prices and stuck government budgets.
Another piece says 'everything is going wrong' for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
stories.vc: Political trouble in Europe and strain in the Gulf both matter: Gulf money backs many VC funds, and global investors are hunting for steadier growth stories like India.
